sources: Queensland Government, Department of Environment, Southern cassowary: lives in tropical rainforest in north Queensland (also New Guinea); can run up to 50 km/h; good swimmers; the inner toe of each foot carries a long dagger-like claw; males incubate the bright green eggs for about 50 days and raise the striped chicks for about nine months; disperses the seeds of many rainforest plants; most attacks on people happen after cassowaries have been fed; https://environment.desi.qld.gov.au/wildlife/animals/living-with/cassowaries

San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, Cassowary: inner claw up to about 4 inches (10 cm) long; casque on the head; one of the heaviest birds, after ostriches; https://animals.sandiegozoo.org/animals/cassowary
Natural History Museum (London), Birds are dinosaurs: modern birds are living theropod dinosaurs; https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/how-dinosaurs-evolved-into-birds.html

beats.say: Each foot hides a dagger, about four inches long.
It lives deep in the rainforests of northern Australia.
Almost as tall as a person, with a bright blue face.
The southern cassowary. A helmet on its head.
Corner it, and it kicks with that dagger claw.
And it can run up to thirty miles an hour.
Most attacks happen after people feed them.
So I watched from far away. Very far.
A dinosaur-looking bird, with knives for toes.
It's one of the heaviest birds on Earth.
Only ostriches weigh more.
It can't fly, but it's a strong swimmer.
It mostly eats fruit that falls from the trees.
The seeds come out the other end, all over the forest.
So it plants new trees wherever it goes.
And here's the twist. Mom lays the eggs, and walks away.
Dad sits on them, for about fifty days.
Then he raises the striped chicks for about nine months.
Birds are living dinosaurs. This one looks the part.
Would you walk through its rainforest?
A single dad with a blue face and daggers on his feet.
Follow me. Next, an animal with cube-shaped poop.
